Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
- Classification: Resectable upfront  
- Reasoning:  
  • Liver disease consists of two synchronous metastases, 2.2 cm (segment II) and 3 cm (segment V), both ≤3 cm and limited to two segments – criteria compatible with technical resectability (preservation of ≥2 contiguous segments, adequate inflow/outflow, and likely FLR > 30%).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • Molecular profile (RAS‑wild type, MSS) does not preclude surgery.  
  • The primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction) and therefore requires resection; the hepatic lesions are small enough to allow a limited (segmental) hepatectomy that can be combined with the colon operation without needing portal vein embolisation or major hepatectomy.  
  • Although some imaging details (vascular contact, FLR ratio, liver MRI) are missing, the available data do not suggest any contraindication; the missing items are not decisive for declaring the disease unresectable.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Urgent colon surgery – perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or left hemicolectomy) to relieve the obstructive sub‑occlusive syndrome.  
2. Simultaneous limited liver resection – in the same operative session, conduct non‑anatomical or segmental resections of segment II and segment V lesions (or a left lateral and a limited right anterior segmentectomy). This approach avoids a second laparotomy, shortens overall treatment time and is supported when liver disease is minor and the colorectal resection is not extensive.  
3. Intra‑operative assessment – use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location, exclude additional occult metastases, and verify vascular/biliary anatomy; obtain frozen sections if needed to ensure R0 margins.  
4. Post‑operative systemic therapy – after recovery, give adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) because the primary is at least stage III (obstructive lesion) and there is synchronous metastatic disease, aiming to eradicate micrometastatic disease and reduce recurrence risk.  
5. Surveillance – monitor CEA levels and perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT at 3‑month intervals for the first year, then every 6 months, to detect early recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final operative planning)  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio – quantitative assessment (CT volumetry or MRI) to confirm that ≥20‑30 % functional liver will remain after resection of segments II and V.  
- Vascular and biliary involvement – precise description of any portal/hepatic vein or biliary duct contact/invasion that could affect the safety of segmental resection.  
- Liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast – to delineate lesion borders, detect additional sub‑centimetric metastases, and clarify arterial anatomy.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor – important for prognostication and may influence the intensity of adjuvant therapy.  
- Confirmation of no prior systemic therapy – to ensure that the patient has not already received neoadjuvant chemotherapy that could have altered tumor biology or liver parenchyma.  

Obtaining these pieces of information before definitive surgery will solidify the operative plan and minimise intra‑operative surprises.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Classification: Resectable upfront  

Reasoning:  
- Liver metastasis: single peripheral lesion, 2.5 cm, located in segment VI (LiverMetastasesCharacterization – NumberOfMetastases = 1; MaximumLesionDiameter = 2.5 cm; HepaticSegmentsInvolved = segment VI). No reported vascular or biliary invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion = Missing, but absence of any mention makes a vascular encasement unlikely). A segmental or wedge resection will leave an ample future liver remnant, so FLR adequacy is not a limiting factor.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease (All ExtrahepaticInvolvement = False).  
- Primary tumor is in the right colon, discovered incidentally and appears asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation or bleeding reported). Such primaries are routinely resectable with a right hemicolectomy.  
- The MDT already described the case as “suitable for combined surgical treatment,” supporting the view that both lesions can be removed in a single operative session.  

Because the available data already satisfy the technical criteria for curative resection and no decisive missing information (e.g., FLR < 30 % or unresectable vascular involvement) is identified, the disease is classified as Resectable upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain a liver‑specific MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) to confirm the solitary nature of the segment VI lesion and to assess arterial/portal anatomy (addresses Missing – ArterialAnatomy, PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion).  
   - Review colonoscopy and pathology to determine tumor grade and confirm resectability of the primary (addresses Missing – GradeOfDifferentiation, PrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization).  

2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   - Perform a right hemicolectomy (or ileocecal resection) with adequate lymphadenectomy for the primary tumor.  
   - Perform a non‑anatomical wedge resection or segment VI segmentectomy achieving R0 margins (≥1 mm). Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to verify lesion location and exclude occult metastases.  

3. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Given the KRAS‑mutated status, anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated. Plan adjuvant chemotherapy with an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) ± bevacizumab for 6 months after recovery from surgery, as recommended for stage III/IV disease with resected metastasis.  
   - If postoperative pathology shows high‑risk features (poor differentiation, N‑positive nodes, lymphovascular invasion), consider adding a biologic (bevacizumab) to the adjuvant regimen.  

4. Post‑operative surveillance  
   - Serial CEA measurements (baseline 35 ng/mL) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen at 6 months, then annually, or MRI of the liver if CEA rises.  

5. Multidisciplinary follow‑up  
   - Review pathology and postoperative recovery at a MDT meeting to confirm that no additional liver lesions were missed and to finalize adjuvant therapy decisions.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (affects need for adjuvant chemotherapy intensity).  
- Confirmation that the primary tumor has not already been resected (determines whether a simultaneous or staged approach is required).  
- Detailed vascular involvement and arterial anatomy of the liver lesion (critical for planning safe hepatic resection).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetry (ensures hepatic safety, although unlikely to be limiting for a segment VI resection).  
- Presence of a pre‑operative systemic chemotherapy regimen (could influence timing of surgery).  
- Liver MRI results (to rule out additional occult metastases).  

These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative schedule.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the liver lesion appears technically resectable (single 1.8 cm metastasis in segment III), but definitive surgical planning requires (a) complete thoraco‑abdominal cross‑sectional imaging to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease and to define the exact relationship of the metastasis to hepatic vessels/biliary structures, and (b) calculation of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume. Both items are listed as “Missing” in the structured analysis and are decisive for confirming that a curative‑intent hepatectomy can be performed safely.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) for the upper‑rectal T3N1 primary, as already discussed in the MDT.  
2. During the 2‑3 week interval after radiotherapy, obtain the missing staging studies:  
   – Contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bony metastases.  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast to (i) confirm solitary segment III lesion, (ii) assess vascular or biliary involvement, and (iii) calculate FLR volume.  
3. Re‑review the imaging at a multidisciplinary meeting. If no extra‑hepatic disease is identified, the lesion is away from major vessels, and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a steatotic liver), proceed to curative surgery.  
4. Surgical plan – simultaneous (combined) resection because the liver operation is limited (segment III wedge or anatomical segmentectomy) and the colorectal resection is a low‑anterior resection (TME) with a protective diverting ileostomy:  
   – Laparoscopic or open low‑anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, respecting the 8‑12 week interval after radiotherapy.  
   – Laparoscopic segment III resection (anatomical or non‑anatomical) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins and preserve at least two contiguous liver segments.  
5. Post‑operative care – pathology review of the primary (grade, margin, CRM) and liver metastasis. If R0 resection is achieved, give adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX). RAS wild‑type status permits addition of anti‑EGFR therapy in the adjuvant setting if high‑risk features are present.  
6. Surveillance – CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen (or MRI liver) at 6‑month intervals, and rectal MRI if indicated.

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most critical missing information for finalizing the plan are:  
- Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Liver MRI with contrast to define vascular/biliary anatomy and to calculate the FLR ratio.  
- Confirmation that the primary tumor has not already been resected (currently “Missing”).  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the rectal primary (relevant for postoperative risk stratification).  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical decision can be made.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The three liver lesions (2‑3 cm) are limited to segments IV, V and VI with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no radiologic invasion → technically amenable to non‑anatomic or segmental resection.  
- MDT already judged the metastases “primarily resectable” and a simple liver operation is described as feasible.  
- However, two decisive pieces of information are missing:  
   • Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio to confirm that ≥30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy) of functional liver will remain.  
   • Thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases, which would alter the curative intent.  
- Because these missing data directly impact the safety and oncologic validity of an upfront hepatectomy, the case must be classified as Potentially resectable pending completion of the above assessments (or any other prerequisite such as pre‑operative chemotherapy that may be required to test tumor biology).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out lung disease.  
   - Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR and assess arterial/portal anatomy.  
   - Confirm absence of biliary involvement, portal thrombosis, or other hepatic adverse features (currently listed as Missing).  

2. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   - Given synchronous disease, high CEA (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation, start a standard oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab for 3–4 cycles.  
   - Goal: (a) assess tumor biology (“proof of time”), (b) potentially downsize lesions, and (c) allow early detection of rapid progression that would preclude surgery.  

3. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and repeat FLR calculation.  
   - Verify that all three lesions remain resectable with negative margins and that FLR meets safety thresholds.  
   - Confirm no new extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic imaging.  

4. Surgical sequence  
   - If the primary colon tumor is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding reported), adopt a liver‑first approach:  
        a. Perform segmental/partial hepatectomy of segments IV, V, VI (non‑anatomic or limited anatomical resection) preserving ≥30 % FLR.  
        b. Ensure R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to verify no additional lesions.  
   - After hepatic recovery (≈2–3 weeks) or in the same operative setting if the patient’s physiologic reserve permits and FLR is adequate, proceed to definitive resection of the transverse colon primary (right hemicolectomy or extended transverse colectomy) with standard oncologic lymphadenectomy.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic therapy (e.g., total of 6 months peri‑operative chemotherapy) based on pathological response and postoperative recovery.  
   - Monitor CEA serially; aim for normalization as a surrogate of disease control.  
   - Schedule surveillance imaging (CT chest/abdomen) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – required to confirm that a safe hepatic resection is possible.  
- Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) results – needed to exclude pulmonary metastases that would change the intent from curative to palliative.  
- Primary tumor status and symptomatology – determines whether a simultaneous or staged (liver‑first) approach is appropriate.  
- Arterial and portal venous anatomy of the liver – essential for planning the extent of resection and preventing vascular complications.  
- Presence of biliary involvement or portal thrombosis – would modify the technical feasibility of resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The structured analysis shows 4 peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) with no vascular invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: False) and no extra‑hepatic disease on chest imaging (ExtrahepaticPulmonaryInvolvement: False, Peritoneal/LymphNode/Bone: False).  
- MDT comment states “primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra‑hepatic involvement,” supporting technical resectability.  
- However, key information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing:  
  • Future liver remnant volume (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing) – essential to ensure ≥20‑30 % functional liver after resection.  
  • Thoraco‑CT (ThoracoCTScanPerformed: Missing) – needed to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases.  
  • Liver MRI (Has liver MRI been performed?: Missing) – provides accurate lesion mapping and vascular anatomy.  
- Because the FLR assessment (and thoracic imaging) is a decisive prerequisite, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” Therefore it is Potentially resectable pending completion of these evaluations (or corrective actions such as portal vein embolisation if FLR proves insufficient).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult lung metastases.  
   - Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate all lesions, confirm absence of biliary or vascular involvement, and allow precise volumetric FLR calculation.  
2. Assess resectability after imaging  
   - If calculated FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in a non‑chemo‑injured liver), proceed to surgery.  
   - If FLR < 30 %, plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to hypertrophy the future remnant.  
3. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (given high CEA = 200 ng/mL and synchronous disease)  
   - Initiate 2–3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) ± anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because tumor is RAS‑wild‑type.  
   - Re‑image after chemotherapy to evaluate response and disease biology; lack of progression confirms suitability for curative intent.  
4. Surgical sequencing (once FLR is adequate and disease is controlled)  
   - Simultaneous resection is preferred because the primary is in the sigmoid (left‑sided) and there are no obstructive symptoms reported. Perform sigmoid colectomy (primary‑first) followed by parenchymal‑sparing liver resections (segmental/wedge resections of segments II, III, V, VIII) aiming for R0 margins.  
   - If intra‑operative assessment reveals inadequate FLR despite pre‑op planning, convert to a liver‑first approach: resect liver lesions first, then address the primary after recovery.  
5. Post‑operative management  
   - Pathology review of margins and nodal status.  
   - Adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of 6 months total systemic therapy, including pre‑operative cycles) to address micrometastatic disease.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume – decisive for determining whether the planned parenchymal‑sparing resection leaves sufficient functional liver.  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) results – required to confirm the absence of pulmonary metastases, which would alter the curative intent.  
- Liver MRI with vascular mapping – essential for precise surgical planning, especially to verify the “Missing” arterial anatomy and to detect any subtle biliary involvement.  
- Status of primary tumor resection – needed to decide between simultaneous versus staged (primary‑first or liver‑first) approach.  
- Systemic therapy already administered – influences timing of surgery and assessment of tumor biology.  
These missing items are the most critical to finalize the resectability assessment and to safely implement the proposed treatment plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT reports the liver lesions as “technically resectable,” but critical information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing. Specifically, the future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio has not been reported, and there is no data on vascular contact/invasion that could affect the extent of hepatic resection. Moreover, it is unclear whether the primary colon tumour has already been resected or is causing obstruction, perforation or bleeding. Because these missing items are decisive for planning a safe curative operation, the case must be classified as potentially resectable pending completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
• Initial work‑up  
   – Obtain volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; aim for FLR ≥ 20 % (≥30 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
   – Review the CT/MRI for any hepatic‑vascular contact (middle hepatic vein, portal branches) and confirm that a margin‑negative (R0) resection is achievable.  
   – Clarify primary‑tumour status: perform colonoscopy if not already done, document any obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms, and stage the tumour (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis already done).  

• Systemic therapy (first line)  
   – Because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective; initiate a doublet (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) plus bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) for 4–6 cycles.  
   – Use this interval to assess tumour biology (response of liver lesions, CEA trend) and to allow recovery of the primary colon segment if symptomatic.  

• Restaging after chemotherapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and repeat CT of chest/abdomen.  
   – Re‑measure lesion size, verify that no new hepatic or extra‑hepatic disease has appeared, and re‑calculate FLR.  

• Surgical sequencing (based on restaging)  
   – If the primary tumour is asymptomatic and FLR is adequate, proceed with a simultaneous right hemicolectomy + parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (left lateral sectionectomy ±  wedge of segment IVa) in a single operation.  
   – If the primary tumour is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or FLR is borderline, adopt a staged “primary‑first” approach:  
        1. Right hemicolectomy (open or laparoscopic) with primary anastomosis.  
        2. 4–6 weeks recovery, then repeat imaging; if FLR remains adequate, perform liver resection (segment II/III resection plus segment IVa wedge) possibly after a short interval of additional chemotherapy.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) to induce hypertrophy, followed by delayed liver resection.  

• Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   – After completion of both resections, resume systemic chemotherapy (same regimen) for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative therapy, aiming for disease‑free survival.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio – needed to confirm that a curative hepatic resection can be performed safely.  
- Presence/extent of vascular contact or invasion (especially of the middle hepatic vein and portal branches) – determines whether a parenchymal‑sparing resection is feasible.  
- Primary tumour symptomatology (obstruction, perforation, bleeding) and whether it has already been resected – dictates whether a primary‑first or simultaneous approach is appropriate.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumour – influences aggressiveness and may affect the decision to give more intensive neoadjuvant chemotherapy.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs. metachronous) – helps refine biological risk assessment and the urgency of liver‑first versus primary‑first sequencing.
Reference:

The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.

-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.

• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.

• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Case_Content:
Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The three liver metastases are small (1‑2 cm) and confined to segments VI‑VIII, which can be removed with a right‑posterior anatomical resection while preserving a left‑liver remnant that is usually >30 % of total liver volume. However, the structured analysis lacks a quantified future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and detailed hepatic vascular anatomy (arterial/portal/venous relationships). These pieces of information are decisive for confirming that an R0 resection can be performed safely. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending FLR assessment (or portal vein embolisation if needed) and confirmation of vascular anatomy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) for the upper‑rectal T3 N0 primary (as already planned by MDT).  
• Within 1–2 weeks after radiotherapy, obtain restaging imaging:  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT with volumetry) to define lesion borders, vascular/biliary relationships, and to calculate FLR.  
   – Thoraco‑CT (or chest MRI) to reconfirm absence of pulmonary disease (missing in the analysis).  
   – Pelvic MRI to reassess rectal tumour response and mesorectal fascia status.  
• If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.25 in a healthy liver) and vascular anatomy is favorable, proceed with a liver‑first approach:  
   – Right‑posterior sectionectomy (segments VI‑VIII) with intra‑operative ultrasound to ensure negative margins (R0) and preservation of inflow/outflow for the remaining liver.  
   – No need for portal vein embolisation given the limited resection volume, but embolisation remains an option if FLR is borderline.  
• Allow 4–6 weeks for hepatic recovery; then perform total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection) with TME, using the interval to complete any remaining radiotherapy (if consolidation TNT is chosen) or to start peri‑operative chemotherapy.  
• Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) plus anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild‑type status, to treat micrometastatic disease and reduce recurrence risk.  
• Follow‑up: CEA monitoring, 3‑month imaging (CT or MRI) for the first year, then 6‑monthly surveillance.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetric measurement – essential to confirm that the planned right‑posterior resection leaves sufficient functional liver.  
• Detailed hepatic arterial, portal and hepatic vein anatomy (presence of vascular contact or invasion) – required to plan safe transection and to anticipate need for vascular reconstruction or PVE.  
• Liver MRI (or high‑quality contrast‑enhanced CT) – to characterize lesions, detect occult disease, and provide accurate volumetry.  
• Thoraco‑CT (or chest MRI) – to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases that were only “Missing” in the analysis.  
• Status of primary tumour resection (has it already been removed?) and tumour grade – relevant for timing of colorectal surgery and for prognostic assessment, though less directly decisive for hepatic resectability.
Reference:

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The liver lesion is solitary (1 metastasis, 2.7 cm) in segment IVb, which is anatomically favorable for curative resection. However, decisive information required to confirm technical feasibility is missing: (a) a liver‑specific MRI to define vascular/biliary anatomy and confirm absence of vascular contact or invasion, and (b) an assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. In addition, the status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms) is not reported. Because these items directly impact whether an immediate operation can be performed safely, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete staging work‑up  
 – Perform a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including liver‑specific contrast) to delineate the relationship of the metastasis to hepatic vessels, bile ducts and to verify that no additional occult lesions are present.  
 – Calculate the FLR volume (CT‑based volumetry or MRI) and ensure an FLR ≥ 30 % (or FLR/BW ≥ 0.5 %) for a safe resection of segment IVb.  
 – Confirm the primary tumour status: colonoscopy with biopsy, assess for obstruction, bleeding or perforation, and stage the primary (CT‑chest/abdomen/pelvis).  

• Decision on sequencing (based on the above results)  
 – If the primary tumour is asymptomatic, resectable, and the FLR is adequate, proceed with a simultaneous resection (left‑sided colectomy + segment IVb hepatectomy) – this avoids two separate operations and is supported by the literature that simultaneous resection is safe when the liver resection involves < 3 segments and the patient has acceptable comorbidity.  
 – If the primary tumour is symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) or the FLR is borderline, adopt a staged approach:  
  1. Resection of the primary colon cancer first (or diverting stoma if needed).  
  2. Re‑assess liver after recovery; if FLR remains insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) to hypertrophy the remnant, then perform the hepatic resection.  

• Systemic therapy  
 – Given synchronous disease, a peri‑operative chemotherapy regimen (e.g., 3 months neoadjuvant FOLFOX ± biologic, followed by surgery, then 3 months adjuvant FOLFOX) is reasonable, especially if the primary is resected first.  
 – If upfront surgery is performed (simultaneous resection) and the pathology shows low‑risk features (well‑to‑moderate differentiation, negative margins), adjuvant chemotherapy alone (6 months FOLFOX) may be sufficient.  

• Post‑operative follow‑up  
 – Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect recurrence early.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
• Liver MRI (vascular and biliary anatomy, detection of additional lesions).  
• Quantitative FLR ratio or volumetric assessment.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumour (already resected or still in situ, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
• Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumour (to refine risk stratification).  
• Any vascular or biliary involvement of the liver metastasis (to confirm that a margin‑negative resection is feasible).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis located in segment IVb, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion is anatomically favorable for a a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary metastasis with favorable anatomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm the relationship of the lesion to segment IVb vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology, however the KRAS status is unknown.
• BRAF wild-type and MSS status do not modify the surgical indication.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT. 

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment IVb wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures (Wisneski et al.; Kim et al.) However, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. K-Ras status, grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Man, 61 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor with two contiguous liver metastases in segment VI (2.1 and 2.4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 180 ng/mL, KRAS mutation.
MDT Discussion: Limited and accessible liver involvement, no indication for upfront chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
• The two liver lesions (2.1 cm and 2.4 cm in segment VI) are small, contiguous and technically amenable to a parenchyma‑sparing segmentectomy, satisfying the technical criteria for resection (ability to preserve ≥2 contiguous segments, vascular inflow/outflow, biliary drainage).  
• However, decisive information is missing: (a) thoraco‑CT (or other chest imaging) to rule out pulmonary metastases, (b) liver MRI (or detailed arterial/portal anatomy) to confirm absence of vascular involvement, and (c) a calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. 1. Complete staging work‑up  
   – Obtain a thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude extra‑hepatic pulmonary disease.  
   – Perform a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or at least a triphasic CT with arterial phase) to delineate vascular anatomy, confirm lack of portal/hepatic vein involvement and calculate the FLR volume.  
2. Evaluate the primary sigmoid lesion  
   – Confirm that the primary tumor has not yet been resected and assess for obstruction, perforation or bleeding. If asymptomatic, proceed to combined (simultaneous) resection; if symptomatic, prioritize colon resection first.

   – Simultaneous resection: laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) together with a laparoscopic or open segment VI metastasectomy (non‑anatomic wedge or segmentectomy) aiming for R0 margins. 4. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   – No neoadjuvant chemotherapy is indicated per MDT discussion because disease is limited and biologically favorable (KRAS‑mutated but no high‑risk features).  
   – Offer standard adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) after recovery from surgery, guided by oncologic protocols and patient performance status.

• Thoraco‑CT (or equivalent chest imaging) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
• Liver MRI (or detailed arterial/portal phase imaging) to assess vascular contact/invasion and to calculate the FLR ratio.  
• FLR ratio or volumetric assessment to ensure postoperative liver function.  
• Confirmation of whether the primary sigmoid tumor has already been resected and its symptom status (obstruction, perforation, bleeding).  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Woman, 66 years old, high rectal T3N1 cancer with a single 1.5 cm metastasis in segment II at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 50 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Peripheral resectable metastasis, possibility of combined surgery after pelvic treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The liver lesion is a solitary 1.5 cm metastasis in segment II, which is technically amenable to a non‑anatomic wedge resection preserving a sufficient future liver remnant.  
 The primary rectal tumor is T3N1 and, according to standard rectal cancer algorithms, requires neoadjuvant chemoradiation (or total neoadjuvant therapy) before any definitive resection; therefore surgery cannot be performed “upfront.”  
 A decisive piece of information is missing: thoracic imaging (CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases, and liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular or biliary involvement and to calculate the FLR ratio. Without this data the safety of a curative resection cannot be guaranteed, so the case is classified as potentially resectable pending completion of those steps.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary – initiate total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT):  
    Induction systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles FOLFOX ± biologic given RAS‑wild‑type) → followed by long‑course chemoradiation (50.4 Gy with concurrent 5‑FU/Capecitabine).  
2. Restaging after TNT – obtain:  
    High‑resolution pelvic MRI to assess tumor response and circumferential resection margin.  
    Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or liver‑specific MRI) to verify that the segment II lesion remains ≤2 cm, without vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate the FLR ratio.  
    Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
3. Multidisciplinary decision – if restaging shows:  
    Good response of the rectal tumor (no threatening MRF, resectable) and stable or regressed liver lesion, and no extra‑hepatic disease, proceed to curative surgery.  
4. Surgical plan – because the liver resection is minor (segment II wedge) and the rectal resection is a low‑anterior resection (TME), a simultaneous laparoscopic approach is feasible:  
    Laparoscopic low‑anterior resection with total mesorectal excision and protective loop ileostomy (if indicated).  
    Laparoscopic or open non‑anatomic wedge resection of segment II with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins.  
    Ensure at least 2 contiguous liver segments remain with adequate inflow/outflow and a FLR ≥ 30 % (to be confirmed intra‑operatively).  
5. Post‑operative management –  
    Pathology‑driven adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of planned systemic regimen).  
    Consider adjuvant targeted therapy (anti‑EGFR) if further molecular profiling supports benefit.  
    Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and MRI pelvis at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
 Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) results – essential to exclude pulmonary metastases that would change the intent from curative to palliative.  
 Liver MRI with vascular mapping – required to rule out hidden vascular/biliary involvement and to calculate the future liver remnant ratio.  
 Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to confirm that resection of segment II will leave an adequate functional liver volume.  
 Status of primary tumor resection – currently “Missing”; confirmation that the rectal primary has not yet been removed is needed to schedule neoadjuvant therapy.  
 Tumor differentiation grade – while not directly altering resectability, it informs prognosis and may influence the intensity of systemic therapy.  
 Timing of liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) – clarifies whether the lesion is truly synchronous, which impacts sequencing decisions.  

These missing items should be obtained before finalizing the surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left T4aN2 colon cancer, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Max size 3.8 cm. CEA 330 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Limited liver involvement, potentially curative upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The three liver lesions (segments IV, V, VIII, largest 3.8 cm) could be removed with curative intent, but the structured analysis lacks a definitive FLR‑ratio assessment and any evaluation of vascular or biliary involvement that could make the resection technically unsafe.  
 Thoraco‑CT has not been performed, so occult pulmonary metastases cannot be excluded.  
 The status of the primary colon tumour (resected or not) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms are missing, which influences the sequencing of surgery.  
 Because these missing pieces of information are decisive for planning a safe hepatectomy, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the required assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Complete staging  
    Perform thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary disease.  
    Obtain liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion vascular contact, biliary involvement, and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
    Review colonoscopy and operative notes to confirm whether the primary tumour has already been resected; if not, assess for obstruction, perforation or bleeding.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
    Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, given the KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
    Treat for 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles) to assess tumour biology, control micrometastatic disease and possibly down‑size the liver lesions.  

3. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
    Repeat liver MRI (or triphasic CT) to evaluate response, confirm FLR adequacy and re‑measure lesion size.  
    If FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy), plan portal‑vein embolisation (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS, depending on the degree of hypertrophy needed.  

4. Surgical sequencing  
    If the primary tumour is still in situ and asymptomatic:  
     – Perform a colon‑first approach (segmental left‑sided colectomy) followed by recovery (≈ 4–6 weeks).  
     – Continue postoperative chemotherapy (same regimen) for additional 2–3 months to maintain disease control.  
    If the primary tumour is symptomatic or at high risk of obstruction/perforation: proceed with colon resection first, as above.  
    If the primary tumour has already been resected or is low‑risk, a simultaneous resection can be considered only when the liver operation is limited (e.g., non‑major wedge resections). In this case, the lesions involve both lobes, likely requiring a right hepatectomy plus segment IV wedge – a major resection – so a staged approach is safer.  

5. Definitive liver surgery  
    Aim for an R0 resection of all three metastases, preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
    Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and to guide parenchymal transection.  
    If FLR is adequate after any pre‑operative hypertrophy manoeuvre, proceed with right hepatectomy (segments V‑VIII) plus non‑anatomical resection of segment IV.  

6. Post‑operative management  
    Pathology review of both primary and liver specimens (including margin status, differentiation, lymphovascular invasion).  
    Resume/adapt adjuvant chemotherapy for a total of 6 months (or longer if high‑risk features persist).  
    Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
 Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – without a quantified FLR the safety of a major hepatectomy cannot be confirmed.  
 Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) results – needed to exclude pulmonary metastases that would alter the curative intent.  
 Primary tumour resection status and symptomatology – determines whether a colon‑first, simultaneous, or liver‑first sequence is appropriate.  
 Liver MRI (vascular/biliary involvement) – essential to plan the extent of hepatic resection and to decide if portal‑vein embolisation or a staged approach is required.  
 Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been given – influences timing of surgery and the need for additional neoadjuvant cycles.

Woman, 52 years old, T3N2 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with bilobar liver metastases (six lesions, 2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 600 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: invasion of the middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, goal of volumetric reduction with chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The liver disease is currently deemed “not initially resectable” because of bilobar distribution, six lesions (2‑5 cm) and documented invasion of the middle hepatic vein – a vascular involvement that compromises a safe R0 resection and threatens an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
 The MDT explicitly stated that the goal is “volumetric reduction with chemotherapy,” indicating that conversion therapy is required before a definitive hepatectomy can be attempted.  
 A decisive missing piece is the FLR‑ratio (future liver remnant compatibility with surgery); without this information the feasibility of a one‑stage resection cannot be confirmed. Therefore the case fits the definition of “potentially resectable” (requires down‑staging chemotherapy and FLR assessment before surgery).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
    Initiate an effective first‑line doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated).  
    Plan for at least 4 cycles (≈2 months) before the first radiologic reassessment; continue up to 6 cycles if response is insufficient, respecting the 6‑month total duration recommended for conversion therapy.  

2. Restaging after chemotherapy  
    Repeat high‑quality liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and triphasic CT to evaluate:  
     – Tumour size reduction and number of viable lesions.  
     – Persistence or regression of middle hepatic vein invasion.  
     – Precise hepatic segment involvement and arterial/portal anatomy.  
    Calculate FLR volume (CT‑volumetry); target >30 % of total liver volume in a chemotherapy‑naïve liver or >40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected.  

3. If FLR is insufficient or vascular involvement persists  
    Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches (or left, depending on planned resection) to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
    Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH):  
     – Stage 1: clearance (resection or ablation) of all lesions in the intended FLR, followed by PVE.  
     – Interval (≈4–6 weeks) with possible continuation of systemic therapy.  
     – Stage 2: completion right (or extended right) hepatectomy once FLR hypertrophy is adequate.  

4. Surgical approach to the liver  
    Aim for an R0 resection; if marginal vascular contact remains, a parenchymal‑sparing resection with R1 vascular margin is acceptable in KRAS‑mutated disease (see literature on R1 vascular resection).  
    Intra‑operative ultrasound and possible use of fiducial markers (if disappearing lesions are suspected) to ensure complete clearance.  

5. Management of the primary rectal tumour  
    Upper‑third rectal cancer does not routinely require radiotherapy; incorporate the rectal primary into the total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) sequence using the same systemic regimen.  
    After liver disease is controlled and the patient is deemed operable, perform a low anterior resection (LAR) with total mesorectal excision, preferably after the hepatic stage (liver‑first strategy) to avoid delaying liver‑directed therapy.  
    If the primary becomes symptomatic or shows progression, consider short‑course radiotherapy before resection, but this is not mandatory given the current asymptomatic status.  

6. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
    Complete the planned peri‑operative chemotherapy (additional 3–6 cycles) after hepatic and colorectal resections, following the EORTC 40983 (EPOC) protocol, to improve disease‑free survival.  

7. Surveillance  
    Serial CEA measurements (baseline 600 ng/mL) and imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or MRI liver) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, to detect early recurrence.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
 FLR‑ratio compatibility with surgery – required to decide between one‑stage resection, PVE, or two‑stage approach.  
 Exact hepatic segments involved and arterial/portal anatomy – needed to plan the extent of resection and feasibility of vascular reconstruction or parenchymal‑sparing techniques.  
 Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) – influences the urgency of systemic therapy and choice of liver‑first versus classical sequence.  
 Whether any systemic therapy has already been administered – determines cumulative chemotherapy exposure and liver functional reserve.  
 Status of the primary tumour (resected or not) – impacts sequencing of colorectal versus hepatic surgery.  
 Brain imaging result – although extra‑hepatic disease is assumed absent, a missing brain assessment could uncover occult metastasis that would alter curative intent.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metachronous metastases, anatomically accessible, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The two liver lesions (2.8 cm in segment V and 3.2 cm in segment VIII) are anatomically amenable to curative‑intent resection (segmentectomy or wedge resection) and there is no documented extra‑hepatic disease.  
 However, the structured analysis lists FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio: Missing. An adequate FLR (≥30 % of total liver volume in a normal liver, ≥40 % if steatosis or prior chemotherapy) is a decisive technical criterion; without this information the surgeon cannot confirm that a safe resection is possible.  
 Consequently the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending clarification of FLR and any vascular/biliary involvement.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete pre‑operative assessment  
    Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR.  
    Evaluate hepatic vasculature and biliary anatomy (CT‑angiography or MR‑angiography) to rule out portal/hepatic vein invasion.  
    Obtain baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available) and performance‑status assessment (ECOG/ASA).  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (because KRAS is mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are not indicated)  
    Initiate a standard doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab for 2–3 months.  
    Rationale: high CEA (180 ng/mL) suggests biologically active disease; peri‑operative chemotherapy provides “proof of time” and may improve disease‑free survival, as supported by the literature on metachronous CRLM.  

3. Restaging after chemotherapy  
    Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) to assess tumor response and verify that no new lesions have appeared.  
    Re‑measure FLR after any chemotherapy‑induced liver injury; if FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the future remnant.  

4. Surgical resection (provided FLR ≥ 30 % and no vascular invasion)  
    Perform an anatomic segment V and segment VIII resection or parenchymal‑sparing wedge resections aiming for R0 margins.  
    Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude occult disease.  

5. Post‑operative management  
    Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative cycles).  
    Monitor CEA every 1–2 months and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
 Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio – required to confirm technical feasibility of resection.  
 Presence of vascular or biliary involvement – would alter the operative plan or render the disease unresectable.  
 Baseline liver function and performance status – needed to assess surgical fitness and risk of postoperative liver failure.  
 Details of prior systemic therapy (if any) – influence choice of neoadjuvant regimen and timing.  
 Primary tumor pathology (grade, margin status, perineural/vascular invasion) – provide additional prognostic information that may affect the decision to give adjuvant therapy.

Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous metastases, potentially curable, negative extra-hepatic workup.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
• The liver lesions are few (2) and small (largest 2.5 cm) and there is no documented extra‑hepatic disease, which from the analysis (ExtrahepaticPeritonealInvolvement = False, ExtrahepaticLymphNodeInvolvement = False, ExtrahepaticBrainInvolvement = False) would favour resection.  
• However, decisive technical information is missing: • FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery is marked “Missing”; without a volumetric assessment we cannot confirm that a safe future liver remnant (≥30 % in a 70‑year‑old) will remain after resection of segments II and V.  
• PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion and arterial anatomy are also “Missing”, which could preclude a parenchyma‑sparing resection or require vascular reconstruction.  
• Thoraco‑CTScanPerformed is “Missing”, so occult pulmonary metastases cannot be excluded.  
Because these missing items are essential for confirming that an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate liver function, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” – i.e. resection is possible after obtaining the missing data (and, if needed, performing portal‑vein embolisation or a staged approach).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete restaging  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other occult metastases (addresses ExtrahepaticPulmonaryInvolvement).  
   – Perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate the future liver remnant; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in an elderly patient) plan portal‑vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   – Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to clarify vascular relationships (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, ArterialAnatomy) and to measure the size of the segment V micronodule (Missing MinimumLesionDiameter).  
   – Review CEA trend (baseline 95 ng/mL) and any post‑chemotherapy change (CEALevelDecrease = Missing) to gauge biologic response.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if needed)  
   – If imaging shows borderline FLR or equivocal response, give 2–3 cycles of a doublet regimen (FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR, given RAS‑wild‑type) to serve as a “biologic test” and possibly further shrink the lesions.  
   – Re‑image after chemotherapy to confirm disease stability or regression (EvolutionOfMetastasesUnderChemotherapy = Missing).  

3. Surgical plan  
   – Assuming FLR is adequate and no vascular invasion, proceed with a liver‑first, curative‑intent resection because the primary rectal cancer has already been removed.  
   – Perform a non‑anatomic wedge resection of the segment II lesion (2.5 cm) and a segmentectomy or wedge of the segment V micronodule, aiming for R0 margins (>1 mm). Use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any additional occult lesions.  
   – Preserve at least two contiguous hepatic segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage (technical criteria from the literature).  

4. Post‑operative management  
   – Give adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) for 3–6 months, especially given the high pre‑operative CEA, to address micrometastatic disease.  
   – Monitor CEA every 3 months and perform cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery – essential to confirm that a safe liver remnant will remain after resection.  
• PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion and ArterialAnatomy – required to plan the extent of resection and anticipate need for vascular reconstruction.  
• ThoracoCTScanPerformed – needed to exclude pulmonary metastases, which would change the curative intent.  
• Post‑chemotherapy response data (CEALevelDecrease, EvolutionOfMetastasesUnderChemotherapy, MinimumLesionDiameter) – important to judge tumor biology and decide whether additional neoadjuvant cycles are warranted.  
These items are the most critical gaps that must be addressed before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Case_Content:
Man, 67 years old, left colectomy for T4N2M0 colon cancer 18 months ago. Surveillance: CEA 380 ng/mL. Liver MRI: four bilobar lesions, 2 to 3.5 cm.thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous liver recurrence, potentially resectable based on volumetric assessment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The liver disease is metachronous, bilobar, with four lesions 2–3.5 cm, which can be technically resected only if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) is left and no major vascular or biliary invasion is present.  
- The MDT comment “potentially resectable based on volumetric assessment” indicates that a key technical factor (FLR) is borderline and has not yet been confirmed (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery is Missing).  
- Biological concerns (CEA = 380 ng/mL, high tumor burden) also favor a “proof‑of‑time” approach with neoadjuvant chemotherapy before committing to surgery.  
- Because a decisive piece of information (FLR adequacy) and a prerequisite systemic therapy are missing, the case fits the definition of “Potentially resectable” rather than upfront resectable.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline systemic therapy  
   - Initiate a modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR, guided by KRAS status when available).  
   - Treat for 2–3 months (or 4–6 cycles) to assess tumor biology (“proof of time”) and to attempt downsizing of the lesions.  

2. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and a volumetric CT to determine:  
      Current size and number of lesions (response).  
      Precise hepatic segments involved.  
      Presence of vascular or biliary contact/invasion.  
      FLR volume; if FLR < 30 % of standardized liver volume, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to augment FLR.  

3. Surgical planning  
   - If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows adequate FLR and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection:  
      Prefer a parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resection of all four metastases aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
      Because disease is bilobar, a staged approach (e.g., right‑sided resection first, then left‑sided resection after FLR hypertrophy) may be required; simultaneous resection is only considered if FLR is sufficient and operative time acceptable.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and to guide any additional ablative adjunct (RFA/ microwave) for lesions in difficult locations.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of adjuvant chemotherapy) based on pathological response and margin status.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to decide whether immediate resection, portal vein embolization, or a two‑stage strategy is required.  
- Exact hepatic segments involved and presence of vascular/biliary contact or invasion – determines technical feasibility of a single‑stage, parenchymal‑sparing resection.  
- Prior systemic therapy status and response – confirms tumor biology and may downsize lesions, influencing timing of surgery.  
- Molecular profile beyond BRAF (KRAS/NRAS, MSI/MMR) and CA 19‑9 level – guides choice of biologic agent and adds prognostic information.  
- Pathologic grade of differentiation and primary‑tumor margin status – affect overall oncologic risk and may sway toward more aggressive peri‑operative chemotherapy.

According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited bilobar metachronous metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

• Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to precisely define the segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships of the 4 lesions.

• Given the high CEA level (380 ng/mL) and early recurrence (18 months), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
