• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the four lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound aiming for R0 margins.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma resected 3 years earlier. CEA 520 ng/mL. at the abdominal CT scan: two liver metastases (segments II and VI), sizes 3.1 and 4.0 cm. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous liver recurrence, anatomically possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- MDT notes “anatomically possible” bilobar recurrence (segments II and VI).  
- However, decisive information is missing:  
   • Thoraco‑CT has not been performed – needed to exclude occult pulmonary metastases.  
   • Liver MRI is absent – required to define vascular/biliary relationship and confirm that lesions are amenable to R0 resection.  
   • Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio is not reported – essential to ensure that resection will leave ≥30 % functional liver (or ≥0.7 %/kg).  
Because these missing data directly affect the feasibility of a curative hepatectomy, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the above assessments (or alternative actions such as portal vein embolisation if FLR proves insufficient).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging before any liver surgery  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out lung metastases.  
   – Perform a liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences to delineate lesion margins, vascular contact, and biliary anatomy.  
   – Calculate FLR volume (CT‑volumetry or MRI) and determine FLR ratio.  
2. Initiate peri‑operative systemic therapy (given high‑risk biology: CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS‑mutated, bilobar disease)  
   – Preferred regimen: 2–3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPEOX) ± bevacizumab (or cetuximab if KRAS wild‑type, but here KRAS mutated).  
   – Goal: “proof of time” to confirm disease stability and treat micrometastatic burden.  
3. Restage after chemotherapy (repeat MRI and thoracic imaging)  
   – If lesions remain resectable, no new extra‑hepatic disease, and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥0.7 %/kg), proceed to hepatic resection.  
   – Surgical plan: simultaneous, parenchyma‑sparing resections – non‑anatomic wedge resection of segment II lesion and segment VI lesion (both ≤4 cm), preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
   – If FLR is inadequate, consider portal vein embolisation of the right portal branch (or left, depending on planned resection) to hypertrophy the future remnant, or a two‑stage approach.  
4. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy for a total of 6 months (adjuvant phase) unless contraindicated.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring (baseline now 520 ng/mL) and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Liver MRI with vascular/biliary assessment.  
- Quantified FLR ratio (or volumetry).  
- Confirmation of any prior systemic therapy (has the patient already received chemotherapy?).  
- Details on vascular contact/invasion of the liver lesions.  
These items are most critical to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive “resectable upfront” plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right colectomy for T3N1 tumor 2 years ago. CEA 140 ng/mL. Liver MRI: three liver metastases (IV, V, VI), sizes 2 to 3 cm. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Limited liver involvement, no other locations.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the three metachronous liver metastases (2‑3 cm) in segments IV, V and VI are anatomically amenable to a parenchymal‑sparing resection, but the Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio is not reported. An adequate FLR (≥20‑30 % of total liver volume in a healthy liver) is a decisive factor for safe hepatectomy; therefore the missing FLR data makes the case “potentially resectable” until this information is obtained (or a pre‑operative maneuver such as portal vein embolisation is deemed necessary).  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Complete restaging: obtain a thoraco‑CT (or chest CT) and a contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT/MRI to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease and to evaluate vascular/biliary relationships of the three lesions.  
- Perform volumetric liver assessment (CT‑ or MRI‑based) to calculate the FLR ratio; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach, otherwise proceed to surgery.  
- Initiate peri‑operative systemic therapy because of the markedly elevated CEA (140 ng/mL) and to test tumour biology: give 4‑6 cycles of a modern doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR agent (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status.  
- Re‑image after chemotherapy; if disease is stable or responding and no new lesions appear, schedule curative‑intent liver surgery.  
- Surgical plan: parenchymal‑sparing segmental resections of segments IV, V and VI (or non‑anatomic wedge resections) aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow. No major hepatectomy is required; therefore portal vein embolisation is unlikely to be needed if FLR is sufficient.  
- Post‑operative management: resume/adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., additional 4‑6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) to address micrometastatic disease, given the high pre‑operative CEA and prior disease‑free interval of 2 years.  
- Surveillance: CEA measurement and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6–12 months thereafter.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- FLR ratio compatibility with surgery (critical for safety of resection).  
- Presence of vascular or biliary involvement of the metastases (needed to confirm technical feasibility).  
- Confirmation that no systemic chemotherapy has already been administered (affects timing of peri‑operative therapy).  
- Detailed pathology of the primary tumour (grade, margin status, lymph‑vascular invasion) – useful for prognostication and to refine the need for adjuvant therapy.  
- Results of thoraco‑CT/abdomen‑CT to definitively exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (especially pulmonary or bone lesions).

Case_Content:
Woman, 74 years old, rectal cancer resected 5 years ago, new CEA elevation to 600 ng/mL. at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: single liver metastasis segment IVa (4.2 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late solitary metastasis, potentially curable situation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The case presents a solitary 4.2 cm metastasis in segment IVa with no extra‑hepatic disease on CT, which is technically amenable to resection. However, decisive information required to confirm feasibility is missing: (a) detailed vascular anatomy and any tumor‑vessel contact/invasion, (b) an accurate assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and (c) high‑resolution liver MRI to delineate lesion borders. Because these pieces of information are essential for planning a safe R0 resection while preserving adequate liver function, the lesion must be considered potentially resectable pending further imaging and functional assessment.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1. Confirm baseline liver status: obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) to define tumor relationship to hepatic veins, portal structures and to calculate FLR.  
- 2. Assess hepatic functional reserve (CT‑based volumetry, indocyanine‑green clearance or similar) and overall performance status.  
- 3. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease) as a “test of time” to evaluate tumor biology and to potentially downsize the lesion.  
- 4. Restage after chemotherapy with repeat MRI and CT; re‑calculate FLR. If the lesion remains resectable with adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % in older patients) and no new vascular involvement, proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery (segment IVa anatomical resection or non‑anatomic wedge ensuring ≥1 mm margin).  
- 5. Perform intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm absence of occult lesions and to guide resection.  
- 6. Post‑operative management: complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic therapy (including postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy) and enroll in intensive surveillance (CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging every 6 months).  
- 7. If restaging shows progression (new lesions, vascular encasement, insufficient FLR), shift to conversion strategies (e.g., portal vein embolisation, two‑stage hepatectomy) or consider local ablative modalities (RFA/SBRT) combined with systemic therapy.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Vascular contact or invasion status of the segment IVa lesion (critical for technical resectability).  
- Quantified future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetric data (critical for functional safety).  
- Liver MRI results (necessary to resolve the above points and to detect occult disease).  
- Confirmation of whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered (to avoid duplicate exposure and to gauge treatment‑induced tumor biology).  
These missing items are the most pivotal for finalizing the surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 68 years old, T3N2 rectal tumor operated 4 years ago. CEA 78 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two metastases segments III and VI (2 and 2.6 cm), no extra-hepatic involvement.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, anatomically simple.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The structured analysis shows two metachronous liver metastases, each ≤ 3 cm, located in peripheral segments III and VI. No extra‑hepatic disease is present. Bilobar disease is limited to a single lesion per lobe, which can be removed with non‑anatomic segmentectomy or wedge resection while preserving a large functional liver remnant. The absence of reported vascular or biliary invasion and the small size of the lesions make a curative R0 resection technically feasible without the need for portal vein embolisation or staged hepatectomy. Therefore, based on the available data the patient meets criteria for immediate surgical resection.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Restaging imaging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen (or repeat liver MRI) to confirm the current extent of disease and to assess the future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
• Molecular work‑up: test the primary tumour (or archived tissue) for RAS, BRAF and MSI status to guide systemic therapy choice.  
• Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but recommended): administer 2–3 months of a standard doublet (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± biologic agent according to molecular profile. This “test of time” will verify tumour biology, may further down‑size the lesions, and allows CEA trend monitoring (baseline 78 ng/mL).  
• Re‑assessment after chemotherapy: repeat liver MRI (or CT) to confirm that both lesions remain resectable, that no new lesions have appeared, and to obtain an accurate FLR calculation.  
• Surgical plan: perform a minimally invasive (laparoscopic) or open liver‑first approach with segmental resection of segment III and segment VI (or wedge resections) aiming for ≥ 1 cm margins. Man, 66 years old, right colectomy for T4N2M0 cancer 24 months ago. FDG-PET: four liver foci, 1.5-3.5 cm, no extra-hepatic. KRAS mutated.

Reasoning: The structured analysis confirms four liver metastases (1.5‑3.5 cm) with no extra‑hepatic disease (Extrahepatic False). However, critical technical information is missing: hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary contact, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery Missing). Without these data the surgical team cannot determine whether an R0 resection preserving ≥2 contiguous segments and an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver) is feasible. Therefore resection cannot be performed upfront and requires further assessment (imaging and possibly liver hypertrophy strategies) before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 - Oncological and surgical sequence  
1. Baseline restaging imaging – obtain high‑quality contrast‑enhanced triphasic CT of the abdomen and liver MRI (gadolinium‑EOB) to define:  
   • exact segmental distribution of the four lesions,  
   • relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles and biliary ducts,  
   • calculate standardized FLR volume.  
2. Multidisciplinary review – liver surgeon, medical oncologist, radiologist, and MDT discuss imaging results and FLR.  
3. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – because KRAS is mutated, initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (or an alternative anti‑VEGF regimen) for 2–3 months. This serves to:  
   • assess tumor biology (response vs progression),  
   • potentially downsize lesions, and  
   • allow time for FLR hypertrophy if portal vein embolization (PVE) is planned.  
4. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – repeat CT/MRI and PET‑CT to evaluate:  
   • radiologic response of each metastasis,  
   • any new lesions,  
   • FLR volume (if PVE was performed).  
5. Decision point:  
   • If all lesions are resectable with an adequate FLR (≥30 % in chemotherapy‑naïve liver or ≥40 % after chemotherapy) and no vascular invasion, proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy. Prefer parenchymal‑sparing, non‑anatomic or segmental resections to preserve liver tissue; aim for R0 margins.  
   • If FLR remains insufficient but lesions are otherwise resectable, schedule PVE (or ALPPS/2‑stage hepatectomy) followed by interval hypertrophy and second‑stage resection.  
   • If disease progresses (new lesions, >3 new lesions, or loss of resectability), continue systemic therapy and consider non‑surgical local therapies (RFA, SBRT) or palliative approach.  
6. Post‑operative management – after R0 resection, resume adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 6 months if tolerated, with regular surveillance (CEA, CT/MRI every 3–6 months).  

Step 3 - Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Hepatic segment involvement and vascular/biliary contact (to judge technical resectability).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume or FLR‑to‑body‑weight ratio (to determine functional safety of resection).  
- Confirmation of whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been given since the detection of liver lesions.  
- Detailed abdominal imaging (contrast CT or MRI) results.  
- Baseline CEA level (useful for monitoring response).  

These missing items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Case_Content:
Woman, 71 years old, left colon cancer operated 5 years ago. Liver MRI: liver lesion segment V, 2.8 cm. CEA 90 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, favorable context, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the solitary 2.8 cm lesion in segment V is technically amenable to a limited anatomical or non‑anatomical resection with preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments. However, definitive surgical planning requires (a) confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease (thoracic CT has not been performed) and (b) assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, which is currently missing. Until these decisive pieces of information are obtained, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases; repeat liver MRI or CT to verify that no additional intra‑hepatic lesions are present.  
- Functional assessment: calculate the FLR volume (CT‑based volumetry) and ensure an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.5 % body‑weight ratio) for a patient with normal liver parenchyma. If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage approach, although this is unlikely for a single segment V lesion.  
- Multidisciplinary decision: if staging confirms liver‑only disease and FLR is adequate, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery. Preferred operation is a segment V anatomical resection (or non‑anatomical wedge) aiming for an R0 margin (≥1 mm). Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to rule out occult lesions.  
- Peri‑operative systemic therapy: given the high CEA (90 ng/mL) and RAS‑wild‑type status, a peri‑operative chemotherapy strategy is advisable. The most common approach is surgery first followed by adjuvant FOLFOX (± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody such as cetuximab) for 3–6 months, as supported by the EORTC 40983 trial for resectable CRLM. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy could be considered if postoperative pathology reveals adverse features (e.g., positive margins, high‑risk primary pathology), but is not mandatory for a solitary small metastasis.  
- Post‑operative surveillance: serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect recurrence early.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Thoraco‑CT (or equivalent chest imaging) to rule out pulmonary metastases – decisive for confirming liver‑only disease.  
- Abdomen‑CT (or full‑body staging) to ensure no additional liver lesions or intra‑abdominal nodal disease.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetry – essential to verify that the planned segmentectomy will leave sufficient functional liver.  
- Detailed primary‑tumor pathology (T‑stage, N‑stage, margin status, perineural/vascular invasion) – important for overall prognosis and may influence the intensity of adjuvant systemic therapy, but not directly required for the immediate resectability decision.

MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, technically accessible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectable upfront  
- The patient has two metachronous liver metastases (2.5 cm in segment II, 3 cm in segment VIII) with no radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Both lesions are small, peripheral and located in different lobes, making them amenable to limited anatomical or non‑anatomical resections while preserving a large future liver remnant.  
- No vascular or biliary invasion is reported; the MDT already judged the disease “technically accessible.”  
- Although the FLR ratio is missing, the planned resection would remove <15 % of total liver volume, which in a normal liver safely leaves >30 % FLR. Therefore the missing FLR data is unlikely to change feasibility.  
- Consequently the case meets technical and oncologic criteria for immediate curative surgery → Resectable upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative phase  
  • Because the CEA is markedly elevated (240 ng/mL) and the tumour is KRAS‑mutated (a poor‑prognosis marker), give a short course (2–3 months) of oxaliplatin‑based doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) ± bevacizumab to obtain a “proof of time” and potentially lower micrometastatic burden.  
  • Restage with contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT after chemotherapy to confirm that no new lesions have appeared and that vascular anatomy remains favorable.  

- Surgical phase (performed after confirming stable disease)  
  • Proceed with a single‑stage, simultaneous liver operation: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment VIII wedge/segmentectomy (or non‑anatomical resections) using intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins (≥1 cm where feasible).  
  • No need for portal vein embolisation or two‑stage approach because FLR will remain >30 % and the resections are minor.  
  • Ensure adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage; close the parenchymal transection with staplers or energy devices as per surgeon preference.  

- Post‑operative phase  
  • Pathology review of resection margins; if R0 achieved, start adjuvant systemic therapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 3–6 months, given the high CEA and KRAS mutation.  
  • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months thereafter.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to confirm that the planned resections will leave a safe functional liver volume.  
- Presence of vascular or biliary contact/invasion – would affect the ability to obtain clear margins and might necessitate more complex resections or vascular reconstruction.  
- Details of the prior rectal resection (margin status, peritoneal involvement, TRG) – important for overall oncologic risk assessment and to decide whether any additional colorectal surveillance or treatment is required.  
- Patient performance status and liver function tests – essential to verify fitness for surgery and chemotherapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a right‑sided T4N2 colon cancer with multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis. Presence of extra‑hepatic disease (brain) makes immediate liver‑first or simultaneous resection unsafe until the brain lesion is controlled and the extent of hepatic disease is fully defined. The structured analysis lacks critical information required to judge technical feasibility (number, size, segmental distribution of liver lesions, vascular/biliary involvement, future liver remnant ratio) and oncologic feasibility (grade, molecular profile, prior systemic therapy). These missing data constitute decisive prerequisites; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending brain‑directed therapy, systemic chemotherapy, and complete hepatic staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Neurologic priority: Arrange urgent neurosurgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery of the cerebellar metastasis, with peri‑operative steroids and seizure prophylaxis as indicated.  
• Primary colon tumor assessment: Determine whether the right‑sided primary is symptomatic (obstruction, perforation, bleeding). If symptomatic, perform diverting colostomy or resection before systemic therapy; if asymptomatic, it can be deferred.  
• Systemic therapy initiation: Start optimal first‑line chemotherapy (e.g., oxaliplatin‑based doublet ± anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR according to RAS/BRAF status once molecular profile is known). Deliver 4–6 cycles to assess tumor biology and achieve possible down‑staging of liver disease.  
• Comprehensive hepatic imaging: Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable) to define number, size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and calculate FLR. Consider PET‑CT for occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Resectability reassessment after chemotherapy: If imaging shows that an R0 resection of all liver lesions is possible with ≥30 % FLR (or FLR/body‑weight ratio >0.5), plan a liver‑first approach. For bilobar disease, consider staged hepatectomy (two‑stage or ALPPS) or portal vein embolization to augment FLR.  
• Primary tumor resection: After successful hepatic clearance (or concurrently if technically feasible and the patient is fit), perform right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy. Simultaneous resection is acceptable only if the primary is asymptomatic and the liver resection can be performed safely (low central venous pressure, adequate hepatic inflow/outflow).  
• Post‑operative systemic therapy: Continue adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or adapted based on response) for a total of 6–12 months, incorporating targeted agents as indicated by molecular profile.  
• Surveillance: Serial CEA monitoring, periodic liver MRI/CT, and brain imaging to detect recurrence.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
- Grade of differentiation and molecular phenotype (RAS, BRAF, MSI) of the primary tumor.  
- Status of the primary tumor: whether it has already been resected and whether it is causing obstruction, perforation, or bleeding.  
- Detailed liver metastases data: exact number of lesions, maximum and minimum diameters, hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and calculated future liver remnant ratio.  
- Confirmation of imaging studies performed (thoraco‑CT, abdomen‑CT, liver MRI) and their findings.  
- Information on any systemic chemotherapy already administered and response achieved.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
- Specific characteristics of the cerebellar lesion (size, edema, mass effect) and planned neurosurgical or radiosurgical treatment.  
- Results of FDG‑PET or amino‑acid PET for detection of additional occult disease.

The presence of brain metastasis indicates advanced systemic dissemination and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

A. Neurological priority (mandatory)
• Immediate neurosurgical and/or radiotherapy assessment of the cerebellar metastasis is required as the first therapeutic step.
• The objective is neurological control and symptom prevention.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT already judged the disease “not resectable upfront” because of six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules. However, resectability could be achieved after (a) systemic down‑staging chemotherapy (and/or targeted therapy) and (b) clarification of key missing technical data (future liver remnant volume, lesion size, vascular involvement, hepatic segment distribution, and detailed pulmonary nodule characteristics). These prerequisites are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, fulfilling the definition of “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT):  
  • Long‑course chemoradiation for the T4 rectal primary (45‑50 Gy with concurrent 5‑FU‑based chemotherapy).  
  • Systemic chemotherapy for metastatic disease: 6‑8 cycles of FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (RAS wild‑type) or FOLFOX + anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) to maximize tumor shrinkage and test disease biology.  
- Restaging after TNT:  
  • High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, number, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
  • Chest CT and FDG‑PET/CT to characterize pulmonary nodules (size, number, metabolic activity) and to exclude additional extra‑hepatic disease.  
- If imaging shows adequate FLR (>30 % in normal liver or >0.5 % / kg body weight) and disease control (≤ 20 % progression, RECIST response), proceed with a liver‑first conversion strategy:  
  • Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS if FLR is insufficient.  
  • Perform a two‑stage hepatectomy (or extended right/left hepatectomy with parenchymal‑sparing non‑anatomic resections) aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous segments.  
- Address pulmonary disease:  
  • If pulmonary nodules are limited (≤ 4, peripheral, amenable to wedge resection) and pulmonary reserve is adequate, schedule simultaneous lung metastasectomy during the second liver stage or a staged thoracic resection after hepatic surgery.  
  • If nodules are more extensive or patient fitness dictates, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or percutaneous ablation as alternative local control.  
- After hepatic (and pulmonary, if performed) clearance, complete rectal cancer treatment:  
  • If the primary tumor remains resectable after TNT, perform total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection) 6‑8 weeks after the last radiation dose, ensuring no residual liver disease.  
  • If the primary is still unresectable or symptomatic, consider a diverting stoma followed by reassessment.  
- Post‑operative management:  
  • Resume adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
  • Enroll in intensive surveillance (CEA, CT/MRI, colonoscopy) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameter, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Results of liver MRI (contrast‑enhanced, hepatobiliary) to confirm above.  
- Status of the rectal primary: whether it has been resected, symptom burden (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
- Pulmonary metastasis specifics: number of nodules, maximum size, lobar distribution, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and presence of mediastinal/hilar nodes.  
- FDG‑PET/CT findings to rule out additional extra‑hepatic disease and to gauge metabolic response.  
- Confirmation of whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These items directly influence the feasibility of achieving an R0 resection with adequate liver reserve and safe simultaneous or staged lung surgery, and therefore must be obtained before proceeding.

• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of a single bone metastasis makes the disease oligometastatic but not curable without systemic control of the extra‑hepatic site. Curative hepatic resection therefore cannot be performed immediately; it requires (a) down‑staging of the liver lesions with systemic chemotherapy and (b) decisive information that is currently missing – namely the number, size and vascular/biliary involvement of the liver metastases and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. Until these data are obtained and a response is demonstrated, surgery cannot be planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy tailored to KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., oxaliplatin‑based doublet such as CAPOX or FOLFOX combined with bevacizumab).  
- Add bone‑directed therapy: palliative radiotherapy to the right iliac lesion (if symptomatic or at risk of fracture) and consider bisphosphonate or denosumab for skeletal protection.  
- Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of chemotherapy:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT with liver protocol) to define number, maximal diameter, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   • Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   • Repeat bone imaging (CT/MRI) to assess response of the iliac lesion.  
- If imaging shows a sufficient FLR (≥30 % in a normal liver or ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury) and all liver lesions are resectable with negative margins, proceed to a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   • Major hepatectomy encompassing segments IV, V and VIII (extended right hepatectomy) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm resectability.  
   • If FLR is inadequate, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy before definitive resection.  
- After hepatic resection and recovery, address the primary colon tumor:  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic and no obstruction/perforation, schedule a delayed colectomy (segmental left‑colon resection) after hepatic recovery.  
   • If symptoms develop, consider simultaneous resection only when the hepatic procedure is limited (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy) and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  
- Continue adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen as pre‑operative) for at least 6 months post‑resection, adapting to response and tolerability.  
- If liver disease remains unresectable after chemotherapy, discuss alternative locoregional options (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, Y‑90 radioembolisation, or percutaneous ablation) and maintain systemic therapy.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final decision)  
- Exact number, maximal and minimal diameters of the liver metastases.  
- Presence or extent of vascular (portal/hepatic artery) or biliary involvement.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume or FLR‑to‑body‑weight ratio.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. intact, presence of obstruction, perforation or bleeding).  
- Baseline carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level and other tumor markers.  
- Thoraco‑abdominal imaging to confirm absence of pulmonary or additional extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Detailed characterization of the bone lesion (lytic vs. sclerotic, fracture risk, spinal/neurologic involvement).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin).  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with liver metastases in segments IV, V, and VIII associated with a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis in the context of a left colon cancer. The presence of osseous metastatic disease indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
•Perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Management of bone metastasis
• Integrate radiotherapy and/or orthopedic evaluation for the right iliac lesion depending on symptoms and fracture risk.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform periodic liver MRI and whole-body imaging to monitor response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Role of liver-directed therapy
• Liver surgery is not indicated unless an exceptional systemic response with control of bone disease occurs, which remains unlikely.

E. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

B. Extent and symptoms related to the iliac bone metastasis.
C. chest CT scan

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the current burden (8 bilobar liver metastases + moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis) precludes an R0 resection now, but resectability could be achieved after (a) systemic down‑staging chemotherapy and (b) acquisition of decisive missing information (PCI score, future liver remnant volume, vascular involvement). Both actions are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as first‑line treatment to achieve tumor shrinkage and to test tumor biology.  
- Within 2–3 cycles, obtain restaging imaging: contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT + liver MRI, thoracic CT, and consider FDG‑PET to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Perform diagnostic laparoscopy to directly assess peritoneal disease, record the total peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and evaluate involvement of the hepatoduodenal and hilar ligaments.  
- If imaging/laparoscopy shows a limited peritoneal burden (PCI ≤ 10) and a good radiologic response of liver lesions (≥30 % shrinkage, no new lesions), proceed to a staged curative approach:  
   • Stage 1 – Cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC for peritoneal disease (if PCI acceptable).  
   • Re‑evaluate liver disease after HIPEC; calculate FLR. If FLR < 30 % or major hepatectomy is required, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage clears the future remnant, second stage completes resection).  
   • Stage 2 – Curative liver resection aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
- Address the primary right‑sided colon tumor: if symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or at high risk of complications, perform right hemicolectomy either before systemic therapy (to prevent obstruction) or after liver‑first approach, depending on clinical urgency.  
- After completion of all resections, give adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX) and consider postoperative hepatic arterial infusion or targeted therapy based on molecular profile.  
- If response is inadequate, PCI is high, or FLR cannot be achieved, shift to a palliative intent: continue systemic therapy, consider liver‑directed therapies (radiofrequency ablation, hepatic arterial infusion) and/or best‑supportive care.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Total peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and detailed peritoneal involvement (ligament invasion, morphology).  
- Precise size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of each liver metastasis.  
- Future liver remnant volume/ratio to confirm technical feasibility after planned resection.  
- Status of the primary tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding).  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) to guide targeted agents.  
- Thoraco‑CT or PET‑CT results to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

A. Extent and distribution of peritoneal disease on imaging.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
C. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
E. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
F. Patient’s performance status for staged surgical procedures.
G. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
